content: A cigar is a tightly rolled bundle of dried and fermented tobacco leaves. One end of the cigar is ignited, allowing the smoker to draw the smoke into their mouth through the other end. Most cigar smokers do not inhale the smoke, as inhaling is often considered improper in certain social circles. The English word cigar originates from the Spanish word cigarro, which itself is derived from the Mayan word for tobacco, siyar. Poor-quality cigars are colloquially referred to as dog rockets. Tobacco for cigars is cultivated in significant quantities in countries such as Brazil, the Philippines, Cameroon, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Honduras, Indonesia, Mexico, Nicaragua, and the United States. Cuban cigars, in particular, are iconic and highly regarded. The history of cigars dates back to at least the 10th century, as evidenced by a ceramic vessel discovered at a Mayan archaeological site in Uaxactún, Guatemala, depicting a man smoking a primitive cigar. Christopher Columbus is credited with introducing tobacco smoking to Europe. During his 1492 voyage, two of his crew members, Rodrigo de Jerez and Luis de Torres, reportedly smoked tobacco wrapped in maize husks in Cuba, making them the first European cigar smokers. By the late 16th century, Cuban tobacco seeds were introduced to the Philippines via the Acapulco-Manila trade route, where the climate and soil proved ideal for cultivating high-quality tobacco. In the 19th century, cigar smoking was widespread, while cigarettes were still relatively uncommon. The cigar industry was a significant economic sector, employing many workers before mechanized production became feasible. Even today, many premium cigars are hand-rolled, with some boxes labeled Totalmente a mano (Totally by hand) as a mark of craftsmanship. The manufacturing process of cigars begins with the harvesting and aging of tobacco leaves. The initial stage, known as curing, involves controlling heat and shade to reduce sugar and water content without causing the leaves to rot. This process takes 25 to 45 days and varies depending on climate and storage conditions. The second stage, fermentation, is carefully managed to allow the leaves to age gracefully, enhancing their flavor, burn quality, and aroma. Once properly aged, the leaves are sorted for use as filler or wrapper based on their appearance and quality. Throughout this process, the leaves are moistened and handled with care to preserve their integrity. The aging cycle involves repeated baling, inspection, and re-baling until the leaves meet the manufacturer's specifications. High-quality cigars are still crafted by hand. Skilled cigar rollers, using crescent-shaped knives called chavetas, can produce hundreds of nearly identical cigars daily. The tobacco, especially the wrapper, is kept moist during the rolling process. Once rolled, cigars are stored in wooden molds to dry, and their uncapped ends are trimmed to a uniform size. Properly stored cigars can age for decades under optimal conditions of 70°F (21°C) and 70% relative humidity. Long-term aging, however, may require lower temperatures, such as 40°F, to prevent flavor deterioration. After purchase, cigars are typically stored in humidors to maintain their quality. Even dried cigars can be re-humidified if handled carefully. Premium cigars often use different types of tobacco for the filler, binder, and wrapper. Long filler cigars are of higher quality, using whole leaves throughout, while lower-grade cigars may use chopped tobacco or even tobacco pulp for the wrapper. Some manufacturers blend various tobacco types to create unique flavors. Cuban cigars, for example, often combine tobaccos from different regions of the island to achieve complex flavor profiles. In contrast, low-grade cigars may burn unevenly and produce a less enjoyable smoking experience. Cigars are categorized by their size and shape, collectively known as vitola. The size is measured by ring gauge (diameter in 64ths of an inch) and length (in inches). Common shapes include parejos, which have straight sides and a cylindrical body, and figurados, which are irregularly shaped and considered more challenging to craft. Figurados, such as torpedoes, pyramids, and perfectos, were historically popular but have seen a resurgence in recent years. Some brands, like the Cuban Cuaba, exclusively produce figurados. The flavor of a cigar is influenced by its blend of filler tobaccos rather than the wrapper, although darker wrappers may add sweetness and lighter ones a drier taste. Cigar enthusiasts often describe flavors using terms similar to wine-tasting, noting overtones and undertones such as spice, cocoa, coffee, nut, wood, or berry. The quality of a cigar is not determined by its strength (mild, medium, or full-bodied) but by personal preference. Cuban cigars are widely regarded as the finest in the world, attributed to the unique microclimate of the Vuelta Abajo region in Pinar del Río Province. Cuban cigars are made entirely from Cuban-grown tobacco, with production controlled by the government. Authentic Cuban cigars are labeled Hecho en Cuba (Made in Cuba), with hand-made ones marked Totalmente a mano. Despite their reputation, Cuban cigars are subject to counterfeiting and smuggling, particularly in the United States, where they remain illegal to purchase due to the trade embargo imposed in 1962 by President John F. Kennedy. Cigars have cultural significance and are often associated with celebrations or symbols of wealth. Historical figures such as Winston Churchill, Sigmund Freud, and Ulysses S. Grant were known for their cigar habits, with some even succumbing to tobacco-related illnesses. The phrase Close but no cigar originates from cigars being given as prizes at fairground games.
